messages.author: 38e260fc5780b4d6
messages.subject: timing scaling
parts:
Hi stan team,

I've been playing with a spatial predictive process model, and find that when my number of iterations get high (above about 70) the time it takes to execute the program increases significantly. To try to do some profiling I compiled with the -pg flag, and can see that the number of calls to functions in the stan::agrad namespace increase in a huge way when I go from 70 to 100 iterations (including log_prob_poly, mdivide_left_vv_vari, etc.). I assume this significant increase in function calls is in part what seems to really bog down my runs if my number of iterations gets over 70. 

The data set is fairly large -  2261 spatial cells, but with only 19 knots (so sampling happens with a covariance matrix that is 19 x 19). It is attached in a compressed bzipped format. I haven't noticed this behavior with small data sets that I tried the code with (hence the large attached data set), but perhaps it is just more exaggerated here. 

This is what I find when I run the executable with a seed=1234 for the same data set.

70 iterations
==========
Elapsed time: 60.96 seconds
Number of calls to log_prob_poly: 951

100 iterations
==========
Elapsed time: 1185 seconds (19.75 minutes)
Number of calls to log_prob_poly: 23984


Attached the stan file, data file, and the first 20 lines of the output from the profiler for both the 70 and 100 iteration runs are attached.

Any ideas why this happens if my number of iterations get above about 70? It's not really intuitive to me why this would happen, but I am not all that familiar with how the NUTS algorithm is implemented.

Thanks again for all your help!

Andria

Hi Andria,

Thanks for providing details.

Before looking at timing results for iterations, I would check to make sure the model is converging. I didn't follow through with all your seeds, but with seed=1234, Stan is not effectively sampling any of the parameters (eta, rho, sigma_sq, mu, alpha) at 70 iterations. For 100 iterations with the same seed, it a bit better. What you should be concerned with is the number of effective samples per unit time, not number of iterations per unit time.


Daniel

parts:
What's most likely happening is that adaptation is figuring
out that it needs a smaller step size, which in turn leads to
more steps per iteration. You can investigate this and the number
of steps (exp(treedepth)). The exact iteration numbers at which this happens
may change in the future, but you should continue to see similar
effects. This is the intended behavior.

As Daniel said, you really want to measure n_eff/second, which we
are going to include in the ouptut in v2.0.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] timing scaling
parts:
On Friday, June 28, 2013 3:17:52 PM UTC-4, Andria Dawson wrote:
Hi Daniel and Ben,

That was Bob. This is Ben for the first time on this thread.

So if I understand correctly, this just means that in the 100 iterations case the number of steps per iteration is greater which explains why it takes more time? If my tree depth is say 8 for an iteration, does that mean I expect to call log_prob_poly exp(8) times (or some factor of exp(8))? (Sorry if that's a silly questions, I really am a NUTS newbie.)

Yes, the number of times the log posterior is evaluated depends on the treedepth when constructing a new proposal for the parameters. This is one reason why you should calculate quantities that are interesting but not needed for the log posterior in the generated quantities block. The generated quantities block is only evaluated once per proposal, while the transformed parameters block and the model block are evaluated every time the log posterior is evaluated.

Ben

If my tree depth is say 8 for an iteration, does that mean I expect to call log_prob_poly exp(8) times (or some factor of exp(8))? (Sorry if that's a silly questions, I really am a NUTS newbie.)

Yes, the number of times the log posterior is evaluated depends on the treedepth when constructing a new proposal for the parameters. This is one reason why you should calculate quantities that are interesting but not needed for the log posterior in the generated quantities block. The generated quantities block is only evaluated once per proposal, while the transformed parameters block and the model block are evaluated every time the log posterior is evaluated.
